title: The Final Stage
dateline: The Storm Citadel, the throne hall. The day before.
mood: The day before, Obsidia sits alone in her throne hall and goes over every move she has planned.

hero.alt: Obsidia floats in a black gown with one clawed glove raised, a pink star glowing at her chest and her silver-pink weapon hanging in the air beside her.

segs.t: On this side of the sky, the door was nearly whole.

Obsidia watched it through the eyes of a gray Ender on her prow. The crack had grown into a star of human sky, its four points torn wide. Behind it lay a gray morning, a bay, and a city under its dome.
Her throne hall lay deep among the hanging blocks. No way led into it from outside.
The throne was the ship’s spine. It came up out of the floor and ran on into the dark of the roof. Every block of the Citadel hung from it.
It hummed, low and even. She felt the hum through the seat. She sat where a neck would be.
She lifted one hand, and across the hall her weapon came to her. It hung at her shoulder, its point toward the dark, untouched. Nothing else aboard came to her hand.

media.alt: Obsidia sits back with one clawed glove stretched out, thin red threads hanging from its fingers, lightning in the storm behind her.

segs.t: In the holds the Ultimate Enders stood with their chests open, each packed with lesser Enders. New plate had closed over their shoulders, heavier than before.
“Augmentation approved,” said Obsidia.
Along the holds the chests swung shut. By the humans’ next morning, the door would be wide enough for the body’s first wave.
Through the Ender’s eyes she looked at the dome. For years the body’s raids had come down on that world, until only this city was left.
The humans counted every raid they lived through as a raid beaten. To Obsidia none had failed. It was the cycle, working on a people with nothing to fight it with.
She had no need to set foot on such an insignificant world herself. Even the storm night had been for the seed. After it, her hand would only have spoiled what grew.
“A waste of time,” she said, of going down for them.
Then the humans had begun to fight back with what they believed. No people on any world she had watched end had done that. Since then, more raids had failed than not.
The Enders could not learn. These humans did. Year by year, they killed her Enders faster.
The body could not answer a people that learned. It had no mind to learn with. She had one.
And her storm could not touch them. Loosed on a city, it killed machines that ran on current while it hung over them. A core lit by belief ran on none.
So she had waited, and built a field that could.
It lay asleep in the hum under her. Let out through the spine, it would spread over the whole city. Wherever it reached, aspirant power would go out. Nothing else would.

It had grown from the light her Enders died of, from the pawn’s reports, and from the dead suit on her prow. The pawn had sold last year’s numbers, as if they were stale. They told her how hard the field must press.
For weeks she had laid the hum on that suit. At last it went only into the core, where a pilot’s belief had once burned. Plate and metal it left alone.
The door was the body’s, and it passed one at a time. So the body would go through first, and the humans would fight it.

When the humans broke its army at a hole in their dome, the body began this door and called her in. The Storm Citadel had been sent to crush humanity’s resistance once and for all. When she went in was hers to choose.
So the ship would wait behind the mouth, with the field ready. If the body finished them, she would watch the old ending hold.
If it did not, she would go in once the mouth was clear. For years she had known that light only through Enders dying of it. Tomorrow she could look at it herself.
And tomorrow was the final stage of her experiment. Under every plan lay one want she had never written into any. She wanted to see a different ending.
This morning the line showed the pawn crossing its city to the humans’ Academy. It lived. It had not obeyed.
She let herself think its name. Selena. Late in the year before, an Ender in a burning street had heard a human shout it at the pawn. Her first recall went down the pulse soon after.
The thread had been silent for days. She had stopped paying on purpose.
A paid pawn stays where it is,
she had thought.
An unpaid one comes looking.
Two more reports had come up the thread, unpaid. Then it went still. On the next storm night the line put it on its tower over the Academy. Then on a roof at the far edge of the city. Then back.
Obsidia knew a bearing when she saw one.
“Good,” she said.
In the nest it had had no name.
It had lain at the end of a row of shells that never held, in a small place pressed into the body’s tissue. It slept there curled while its body grew.
She had come back to it more often than the work needed. She changed its face, then changed it again, until it was right. What “right” meant, she could not have said. She knew each time it was not.
On the storm night she had carried it out of the nest herself, and down. Days ago she had stopped at that empty place with the human girl beside her. She had not asked herself why.
Her hand, she found, had come away from the seat. She laid it down again. She did not ask now.
“Someday, when this story nears its end, she too will return to me,” said Obsidia.

The last call would wait until the pawn showed its own form. Then she would send the one call that carried where she sat. A pawn that could take a bearing from two roofs could follow it. She meant it to.
Every move her creation could make, she had already planned. She hoped it would find one she had not.

media.alt: Obsidia looks back over her shoulder among floating shards of glass, a pink star burning at her chest.
media.credit: Official Obsidia character bio art, A Game of Storms

segs.t: Far out past the body, in her hollow, the human girl’s light was burning.
That one would turn too. Obsidia had expected it since she first saw that sleeve. She did not expect it to matter.
The Will expected it as well. It had known what the girl was from the first hour.
Past the prow, the Mother Matrix stirred and settled.

After she marked that light, Obsidia had read back along the pulse. When the body began its door, the Will made its first move. Of every light its Enders died of on that world, the brightest came from two girls who fought as one. Take one, and the other breaks.

So a door had opened inside the humans’ dome, in a corridor of their Academy. Doors cost the Will dearly in there. It reached through for the one with her back to the door. The other stepped in front of her. Either one served.
What it said to her in the vision had gone down the pulse like any order.
“Vexana of The Aspirants, you have reached the end of your future.”
It had named her side before it named her end.
Her star had been lit from that first hour. Obsidia had first seen it the night her ship came through, from the far side of the body. The dark it burned in was the Will’s own.

Then the Will had gone through her memories, the way it looked out through an Ender’s eyes. Obsidia found them in the pulse too. Fireworks at the edge of a dome. A tree, and a head in her lap. A girl with pink hair, laughing.
So it knew what she loved. It let her keep her mind, and it let her keep the star.
A light is easy to watch.
Then it gave her orders.
“The ruins east of the dome. Tonight.”
“The edge of the dome. Before dawn.”
Each one named a place where nobody lived, at an hour when nobody looked. In all those weeks, not one human had seen her face. The Will was saving it.

The doors she came home through were the Will’s too. It saw the plate she carried, and the cracked cores. To the Will, a few machines in a hollow changed nothing, because the end was settled. It had told her so.
The girl kept her star pinned inside her sleeve. She kept to the edge of the rows, so their eyes would not stay on her. She believed the Will saw only what its Enders saw.
She thought cloth was enough.

The Will was keeping her for one day, and it had a use even for her turning. Tomorrow it would show her face by day, over the city, among its Enders. The humans fought on what they believed. Let them see one of their own on the Enders’ side, and see what they believed after.

It would send her where the pink-haired one would see her, and follow her alone. Then it would give her one order, with that girl in front of her. Whatever she did with it, the Will would have what it wanted.
After that, the rule Obsidia had spoken among the rows would do the rest.
The hum went on under the seat.
She had said none of this to the girl. She would say it to no one.
Told, she does what anything does once it learns it is watched,
Obsidia thought.
That I can predict already. Untold, she might do something else.
What the girl meant to do, Obsidia did not know. She did not go looking.
“Someone told me once that we’d be like fireworks,” the girl had said, in the nest.
Obsidia had seen those fireworks, and who stood beside her under them. She had asked the girl about an after. The girl had answered with an ending.
She had sat there all day. On the far side of the crack, dusk was coming on over the bay.
Obsidia laid her palm flat on the spine beside her seat.
“The mouth,” she said.
The hum rose through the seat and changed its note. Somewhere below her, blocks shifted on their holds and settled.
Through the eyes on the prow she watched the body’s flank slide away. The crack came on until it filled the Ender’s sight. Then the Storm Citadel stopped behind the mouth, and waited.
Its storm ran ahead of it and came through a little at a time. Over the bay, clouds gathered where there had been none. Lightning ran through them. Rain began on the water.
From the city it would look like any other storm.
Through the star of sky her storm went on pouring down into the city’s dusk.
